items.text: Variables point at values; `type()` reveals the type
Lists keep order, dicts look up by key, sets keep things unique
A conversation is a list of `{"role", "content"}` dicts

captions.text: Every AI application, from a simple chatbot to a team of agents, moves the same few
kinds of data around.
Text, numbers, lists of messages, and dictionaries of settings.
In this lesson you will learn those building blocks properly, using the exact shapes
that language model APIs use.
You will create variables and recognise Python's basic types.
Format text cleanly with f-strings.
Use lists, dictionaries, and sets, and know when to pick each one.
And build a chat conversation as a list of dictionaries, which is exactly the format
you will send to a model in Module 2.
A variable is a name that points at a value.
Every value has a type, and the type decides what you can do with it.
A string, s t r, holds text.
Prompts, model names, and replies are all strings.
An int is a whole number, like a token count.
A float is a decimal number, like a temperature setting or a price.
A bool is either True or False, with a capital T and F.
And None means no value at all.
It's often used for something that is optional, or not loaded yet.
Here they are in a small script.
Each line creates a variable with the equals sign.
You do not declare the type yourself.
Python works it out from the value.
The built-in type function tells you what kind of value you have.
That is very handy when something behaves unexpectedly.
This is an f-string.
Put the letter f before the quotes, and anything inside curly braces is evaluated
and inserted into the text.
You will build prompts this way all the time.
A name can be pointed at a new value at any time.
And f-strings can format values too.
Colon comma adds thousands separators.
Run it, and you see the three types, the formatted sentence, and the new limit of
two thousand tokens.
Now a classic mistake.
Joining a string and a number with plus fails with a type error, because Python will
not guess how to combine text with a number.
The fix is an f-string, or converting the number with s t r first.
Read the last line of any error first.
It names the problem precisely.
Next, lists.
A list keeps items in order, and you can change it after creating it.
Square brackets create a list.
Here, three user messages.
You read an item by its position, called its index.
Indexes start at zero, so zero is the first item, and minus one is the last.
The len function gives you the number of items.
Append adds to the end.
A slice takes a range.
One colon three means start at index one and stop before index three.
A for loop visits every item.
Wrapping the list in enumerate gives you a running number as well, starting wherever
you choose.
The output shows the first and last message, the count of three, the slice, and then
the numbered list after Bye was appended.
Dictionaries are the most important structure in this whole course.
A dictionary maps keys to values, so you look things up by name instead of by
position.
This dictionary is a chat message.
It has a role, saying who is speaking, and the content, which is the text.
This is the same shape real chat APIs use.
Square brackets with a key read a value, and assigning to a new key adds it.
The get method is the safe way to read.
If the key is missing, you get the default instead of an error.
Now combine the two.
A list of message dictionaries is a whole conversation: a system instruction, the
user's question, and the assistant's answer.
When you call a model in Module 2, this is precisely what you will send.
Looping over it, the f-string pads each role to nine characters, so the output lines
up neatly.
Here is the result, including the aligned conversation at the end.
And here is the error you will meet most often: a key error.
The key content does not exist in this dictionary.
When a key might be missing, use get with a sensible default.
When it must exist, check it explicitly and give a clear message.
You will do exactly that in this module's project.
The third collection is the set.
A set holds unique items, with no duplicates and no particular order.
Turning a list of tags into a set removes the duplicates.
Because sets have no order, we sort the set before printing it, so the output is
predictable.
The in operator checks membership, and on a set it stays fast however large the set
grows.
Sets also support maths-like operations.
Here, the tools an agent requested, minus the tools it is allowed to use, gives
exactly the forbidden request.
Keep this idea in mind.
Tool allowlists come back in the security module.
Three unique tags, membership is True, and delete files is flagged as not allowed.
One last tool for this lesson: comprehensions.
They build a new list or dictionary from an existing collection, in a single
readable line.
Here are three request records, a list of dictionaries, just like a usage log.
This list comprehension reads almost like English.
Take r's id, for each r in records, if r's status is ok.
Curly braces with a key, colon, value build a dictionary instead, here mapping each
id to its tokens.
And without any brackets, the same pattern can feed straight into a function like
sum.
Two successful ids, a dictionary of tokens, and eight hundred and fifty tokens in
total.
Use a list when order matters, like the messages in a conversation, or the steps of
a plan.
Use a dictionary when you look things up by name, like a message, a configuration,
or a record from a JSON file.
Use a set for uniqueness and fast membership checks, like allowed tools or IDs
you've already processed.
And a tuple, written with parentheses, is a fixed group of values that will not
change, such as a tag and its count.
Quick check.
What does this code print?
Pause the video if you need a moment.
The answer is unknown.
The get method returns the default when the key is missing.
Only square-bracket access would raise a key error.
Variables are names pointing at values, and the type function tells you what a value
is.
F-strings are the clean way to build text, and they can format numbers too.
Lists keep order, dictionaries look up by key, and sets keep things unique.
And a conversation is a list of dictionaries, each with a role and some content.
Next lesson: functions, classes, and exceptions, so you can organise this data into
reusable, reliable code.
